notes.content: To become progressively worse.
/dɪˈtɪəriəreɪt/
Air quality has deteriorated since the factory reopened.
deteriorate rapidly; a deteriorating situation
The verb is intransitive here. Say “the situation deteriorated”, not “deteriorate the situation”.
To make something harmful less severe.
/ˈmɪtɪɡeɪt/
Cities can mitigate the effects of heatwaves by planting trees.
mitigate the impact; mitigate the effects
The variety of plants and animals in a place.
/ˌbaɪəʊdaɪˈvɜːsəti/
Clearing forests reduces biodiversity and leaves fewer species able to survive.
Uncountable in most IELTS sentences: “biodiversity is declining”.
To be a possible source of danger or harm.
Rising sea levels pose a threat to coastal communities.
threaten; put something at risk
The subjects and content that a school or course teaches.
/kəˈrɪkjələm/
The curriculum should leave room for both exams and practical projects.
Plural: curricula or curriculums. Do not write “curriculums of a lesson” for a single class; use “lesson” or “syllabus”.
To gain knowledge or a skill through effort or experience.
/əˈkwaɪə/
Children acquire a second language more easily when they hear it every day.
acquire knowledge; acquire a skill
To decide what the evidence shows.
It is hard to draw a conclusion from a study that only lasted one week.
A new idea, method or product, or the act of introducing one.
/ˌɪnəˈveɪʃn/
Innovation in public transport matters more than a faster phone.
Innovation is the noun. The verb is innovate, and the adjective is innovative.
The identification of an illness or problem after examining the evidence.
/ˌdaɪəɡˈnəʊsɪs/
An early diagnosis gives patients more treatment options.
Plural: diagnoses. The verb is diagnose.
A general rise in prices, so that money buys less than before.
/ɪnˈfleɪʃn/
High inflation makes it harder for families on fixed incomes to pay rent.
The state of not having a job, or the number of people in that state.
/ˌʌnɪmˈplɔɪmənt/
Youth unemployment rises when companies stop hiring graduates.
Uncountable. Say “the unemployment rate” when you mean the percentage.
An unfair difference in wealth, opportunity or treatment.
/ˌɪnɪˈkwɒləti/
Income inequality widens when wages stay flat and housing costs rise.
income inequality; social inequality; widen the gap

front.text: A lot of people think that cities are too crowded.

back.text: It is widely believed that cities have become overcrowded.

notes.content: The impersonal pattern is safer in Task 2. In speaking, “a lot of people think” can still sound natural.
Traditions, buildings or objects that are passed from earlier generations.
/ˈherɪtɪdʒ/
Local festivals are part of a city’s cultural heritage, not just a tourist product.
cultural heritage; preserve one’s heritage
The basic systems a place needs, such as transport, power and water.
/ˈɪnfrəstrʌktʃə/
Without better public transport infrastructure, new housing will increase traffic.
Usually uncountable. Avoid “infrastructures” unless you are contrasting several systems.
A relationship in which people, countries or systems rely on each other.
/ˌɪntədɪˈpendəns/
Global supply chains create interdependence, so a strike in one port delays shops elsewhere.
When “not only” starts the clause, invert the auxiliary: Not only does remote work save time, but it also reduces commuting.
Not only does the policy cut emissions, but it also makes city centres quieter.
Do not write “Not only the policy cuts emissions”. The auxiliary has to come before the subject.

back.text: 尽管（后接名词或动名词）

notes.content: Despite is a preposition, so it takes a noun or -ing form. Use “despite the fact that” before a full clause.
Despite the cost, many families still pay for private tutoring.
Despite of is incorrect. Also avoid “despite it is expensive”.

front.text: a lot of / a great deal of

notes.content: Both mean a large amount. “A great deal of” is more formal and usually pairs with uncountable nouns.
The project requires a great deal of public money.
In speaking, “a lot of” is natural. In Task 2, “a great deal of” or “a significant amount of” sounds more academic. Do not use “a great deal of people”; use “a great many people”.

front.text: Kids today spend too much time online.

back.text: Children today spend an excessive amount of time online.

notes.content: “Kids” is conversational. Essays usually need “children” or “young people”. “Too much” can become “an excessive amount of” when the noun is uncountable.
